name: Israel Aerospace Industries
desc: State-owned Israeli maker of military and civil aircraft, UAVs, missiles, avionics and space systems.
capacity_detail: Total revenue USD 7.38bn in 2025 (Defense News Top 100)
markets: Defence exports to Asia, Europe (incl. Germany) and Israel's own forces; civil aircraft conversions and space systems worldwide.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; a global exporter could use F1 hospitality for government and airline B2B relationships.

name: Rafael Advanced Defense Systems
desc: Israeli government-owned defence company developing missile defence, Iron Dome, Iron Beam laser and precision weapons.
markets: Israel Defense Forces plus export customers in Europe, Asia and the US; owns UK-based Pearson Engineering.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; F1 engineering showcase fits a technology-led exporter, though state ownership limits branding.

name: Naval Group
desc: French naval defence group designing and building submarines, frigates and naval systems, majority owned by the French state.
markets: France plus export programmes in India, Brazil, Malaysia and elsewhere; employs staff in 17 countries.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; engineering-prestige platform for export navy customers; already sponsors sailing.

name: KNDS
desc: Franco-German holding of Krauss-Maffei Wegmann and Nexter, building tanks, artillery and armoured vehicles.
ownership: partnership: KMW founding families 50% and French State 50%
markets: Germany, France and NATO export customers in Europe and beyond for Leopard 2, Caesar and armoured vehicles.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; heavy-engineering brand building a pan-European identity could use F1 for recruitment and B2B hospitality.

name: Ukrainian Defense Industry
desc: Ukraine's largest arms maker, producing ammunition, armoured vehicles, aircraft and unmanned systems for Ukraine and partners.
markets: Ukraine's armed forces plus production relocated abroad and joint ventures with NATO-country partners.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; wartime state ownership makes sponsorship unlikely near term.

name: EDGE Group
desc: Emirati state-owned conglomerate of about 25 companies making missiles, drones, munitions, vessels and electronic warfare systems.
markets: UAE Armed Forces plus exports to Angola, Brazil, Indonesia and Europe; owns Milrem Robotics and stakes in SIATT and Condor.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; Abu Dhabi already hosts an F1 race, giving EDGE a home-market showcase for exports.

name: Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa
desc: Polish state holding of over 50 defence firms producing artillery shells, vehicles, air defence and small arms.
markets: Mainly Poland's armed forces, including a PLN 11bn shell contract, with some exports.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; mostly domestic, so F1's global reach offers limited commercial benefit.

name: Peraton
desc: US national security and technology contractor serving space, intelligence, cyber, defence and homeland security agencies.
markets: US federal agencies including defence, intelligence, FAA air-traffic modernisation; about 18,000 staff.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; three US Grands Prix could support recruitment of scarce engineering talent.

name: Turkish Aerospace Industries
desc: State-owned Turkish manufacturer of combat aircraft, helicopters, drones and aerostructures, including the KAAN fighter.
markets: Turkish Armed Forces plus export customers and aerostructure supply to global aircraft makers.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; Türkiye's export push and past Istanbul Grand Prix make F1 a plausible showcase.

name: Diehl
desc: Family-owned German group making missiles, ammunition, aircraft systems, metal products, controls and metering devices.
markets: Defence customers in Germany, Ukraine and India, plus global aviation, metal and metering clients.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; diversified engineering brand with civil divisions could use F1 for B2B hospitality.

name: Roketsan
desc: Turkish maker of guided missiles, rockets and space propulsion, majority owned by the Turkish Armed Forces Foundation.
ownership: state fund: Turkish Armed Forces Foundation 55.5%
markets: Turkish forces plus exports to Bangladesh and other partner countries.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; export-driven but restricted product category limits consumer-facing branding.

name: Navantia
desc: Spanish state-owned shipbuilder of warships and submarines, also building offshore wind structures; owns Harland & Wolff.
markets: Spain, export navies including Australia and Saudi Arabia, and UK shipyards in Belfast, Appledore and Scotland.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; Spanish fan base and Madrid Grand Prix could support recruitment and renewables branding.

name: Makine ve Kimya Endüstrisi
desc: Turkish government-controlled manufacturer supplying weapons, ammunition and explosives to the Turkish Armed Forces.
markets: Turkish Armed Forces and export customers for ammunition and small arms.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; product category and state ownership make F1 sponsorship unlikely.

name: General Atomics
desc: Privately owned US developer of MQ-9 Reaper drones, nuclear energy, fusion research and electromagnetic systems.
markets: US Air Force and allied militaries worldwide, plus energy and research customers in North America, Europe and Asia.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; drone and fusion technology story suits F1's engineering audience and US races.

name: Sierra Nevada Corporation
desc: Privately held US aerospace and defence firm modifying aircraft and building electronics and space systems.
markets: US Department of Defense, NASA and allied militaries; 36 locations in the US, UK, Germany and Türkiye.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; owner-led company could use US Grands Prix for recruitment and government hospitality.

name: Baykar
desc: Private Turkish company making Bayraktar TB2 and Akinci drones, C4I and AI systems; owns Piaggio Aerospace.
markets: Exports Bayraktar drones to Ukraine and many other countries; owns Italian aircraft maker Piaggio Aerospace.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; brand-led, family-owned exporter with a famous product name and international ambitions.

name: Saudi Arabian Military Industries
desc: Saudi state defence company in aerospace, electronics, land and naval systems, wholly owned by the Public Investment Fund.
markets: Mainly Saudi Arabia's armed forces, localising defence production under Vision 2030.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; PIF-owned like other F1-linked Saudi brands, and Jeddah hosts a Grand Prix.

name: Patria
desc: Finnish provider of armoured vehicles, defence and aviation services; 50.1% Finnish state, 49.9% Kongsberg.
markets: Finland, Sweden and other European armies buying Patria 6x6 vehicles; also aviation services.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; Nordic expansion could use F1 for B2B relations, though branding appetite is limited.

name: Nammo
desc: Norwegian-Finnish maker of ammunition, rocket motors and space propulsion, owned by Norway's government and Patria.
markets: Subsidiaries in Nordic countries, Germany, Spain, Switzerland, UK, Ireland and the US.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; ammunition category makes consumer-facing sports sponsorship unlikely.

name: M1 Support Services
desc: US contractor providing aircraft maintenance and support services, including for USAF flight training wings.
markets: US Air Force and other US military aviation programmes.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; domestic services firm; F1 interest mainly as a technician recruitment platform.

name: AM General
desc: US manufacturer of the military Humvee and other heavy and contract vehicles, owned by KPS Capital Partners.
markets: US Armed Forces and allied militaries buying Humvee vehicles.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; Humvee automotive heritage gives a natural motorsport link.

name: DEFEND ID
desc: Indonesian state defence holding led by PT Len Industri, grouping Pindad, Dahana, Dirgantara Indonesia and PAL.
markets: Mainly Indonesia's armed forces, with partnerships with EDGE and other foreign suppliers.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; domestic focus limits value of F1's global audience.

name: Ultra Electronics
desc: British defence and security electronics company in sonar, communications and sensors, owned by Advent via Cobham.
markets: UK, US and allied defence customers; historically about a third of turnover from the American market.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; UK engineering employer could use British motorsport for engineering recruitment.

name: Rohde & Schwarz
desc: German electronics group in test and measurement, broadcast, cybersecurity and military radio communications.
markets: More than 70 countries, with regional headquarters in the US and Singapore; Bundeswehr radio programmes.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; test and measurement brand serves automotive and telecoms clients that follow F1.

name: FN Herstal
desc: Belgian firearms maker, Europe's largest small-arms exporter, owned by the Walloon government via FN Browning Group.
ownership: state-owned: Walloon Region (via FN Browning Group)
markets: Military and law-enforcement customers worldwide; US subsidiary FN America; sister brands Browning and Winchester.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; firearms category makes F1 sponsorship very unlikely.

name: Pilatus Aircraft
desc: Swiss manufacturer of PC-21 military trainers and PC-12 and PC-24 business aircraft, owned by Swiss investors.
markets: Air forces worldwide buying trainers, plus business-aviation buyers in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; premium business-jet buyers overlap with F1's high-net-worth paddock audience.

name: Marshall Group
desc: British privately owned group in aircraft maintenance and modification, land defence systems and fleet solutions.
markets: UK Ministry of Defence and international air forces, plus fleet and property businesses in the UK.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; Cambridge engineering heritage near UK motorsport valley suits talent-led F1 hospitality.

name: UFORCE
industry: autonomous sea, land and air systems
desc: Ukrainian-founded maker of MAGURA sea drones, strike UAVs, ground robots, counter-UAS turrets and C2 software.
capacity_detail: Raised USD 700M Series A at USD 6bn valuation (Nov 2026)
markets: Ukraine plus allied nations in the US, Europe, Asia-Pacific and Middle East; hubs in London, Kyiv and Washington.

signals.raise: USD 700M Series A at USD 6bn valuation (Nov 2026; https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/uforce-raises-700m-at-6-billion-valuation-from-leading-tech-and-sovereign-wealth-funds-to-scale-combat-proven-defence-systems-for-ukraine-and-allied-nations-302937140.html)

rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; newly funded London scale-up could use F1 for profile and engineering hiring.

name: Kela Technologies
desc: Israeli start-up building open-architecture command-and-control software linking sensors, drones, radars and weapons from many suppliers.
capacity_detail: USD 200M round at USD 1.2bn valuation; about USD 300M raised in total (Jun 2026)
markets: Mainly Israel's defence establishment with dozens of deployment points; considering expansion into the US market.
rationale: Defence brands are not yet in F1 but sponsor NFL teams; planned US expansion could use US Grands Prix, though revenue is small.
